title: Lumbini found
hookLine: Ashoka's pillar was found at Lumbini, marking the birthplace

cards: A dig on the flat, hot plain of southern Nepal, close to the Indian border. Workers clear away earth around a stone column standing half buried near a small shrine.
The pillar is broken at the top, and it's plain, no statue, no carving to speak of. But low on the shaft there's writing, in an old script. Someone copies the letters out, line by line.
And the inscription turns out to say, more or less: this is the place. Here the Buddha was born.

teach.b: First, a place the texts remember. In the Sutta Nipata, a sage named Asita hears that a child has been born who will one day awaken, born in a village of the Sakyans, in the Lumbini country.
In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Buddha himself names the place of his birth as one of the places a faithful follower might visit and be moved. So the name was never lost from the scriptures.

teach.h: THE GARDEN SLIPS OUT OF SIGHT.
teach.b: Second, a place that slipped out of sight. As Buddhism faded in India, the garden itself was overgrown, and where exactly it lay became a question rather than a fact. Third, a king's stone answers it.
The pillar that came out of the ground was set up by Ashoka, the emperor met earlier this year.

teach.h: ASHOKA'S PILLAR: HERE HE WAS BORN.
teach.b: His inscription says, in plain words, that twenty years after he was anointed, the king came here himself and worshiped, because here the Buddha, the sage of the Sakyas, was born.
He had a stone pillar raised, and he made the village of Lumbini free of tax, paying only an eighth share of its harvest. Fourth, why this matters. A holy place can rest on memory alone.
This one also has a king's own words, carved at the spot.

teach.h: A NAME BECOMES A PLACE TO STAND.
teach.b: Pilgrims had a name; now they had a place to stand.
Today Lumbini has gardens, a pool, temples built by Buddhists from different countries, and the old pillar, still standing, still saying the same thing.
A sentence in stone, waiting in the ground until someone could read it.

how: Buddhists from different countries travel to Lumbini in Nepal as pilgrims, visiting the garden, the pool, the temple at the birth site and Ashoka's pillar, and some walk on to the other places named in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta.

games.q: you're on the dig in southern Nepal, and the workers have cleared the earth from a broken stone pillar. what tells you this is the place?
o: a golden statue of a baby buried beside it.
an old inscription on the shaft saying here the Buddha was born.
local guides pointing and saying so.
games.why: the pillar carries Ashoka's own words: he came here and worshiped, because here the Buddha was born.

practice: If you have a map nearby, find Lumbini in southern Nepal, just north of the border with India, or simply picture the flat green plain, the pool, the old pillar in the sun.
Then sit with one thought for the rest of the time: the stupas, the chronicles and the golden towers of these weeks all began with a child born here.

wordCard.voice: Lumbini found. The garden of the Buddha's birth, named in the scriptures, then located again by Ashoka's pillar and its words: here he was born. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: the garden in the Sakyan country where the Buddha was born.
